#1
L: Of renunciation, great-armed one, the truth I wish to know, to know, and of relinquishment, Lord-of-the-senses — separately, slayer-of-Keśin.
I: I want to know the truth about renunciation, great-armed one — and about relinquishment too, Hṛṣīkeśa — each taken separately, Keśiniṣūdana.
N: The final chapter opens with a question the poem has left hanging since 5.1-6, where saṃnyāsa and tyāga were already used without being formally distinguished: Arjuna now asks Kṛṣṇa to define each term pṛthak, 'separately, on its own'. Hṛṣīkeśa, 'lord of the senses', is a standing epithet of Kṛṣṇa; Keśiniṣūdana, 'slayer of Keśin', recalls the horse-demon Kṛṣṇa killed in his youth and is rare in the poem, appearing here as the chapter's opening address. Kṛṣṇa's answer, distinguishing the two terms technically, follows immediately in verse 2.
#2
L: The-laying-down of-desire-motivated actions, renunciation, the-wise know; the-giving-up-of-the-fruit-of-all-action, relinquishment, the-discerning call.
I: The wise call giving up desire-driven action 'renunciation'; the discerning call giving up the fruit of every action 'relinquishment'.
N: Kṛṣṇa opens with two technical definitions rather than a value judgment: saṃnyāsa is nyāsa, 'the laying-down', of kāmyāni karmāṇi, 'actions performed from desire' (optional rites undertaken for some reward); tyāga is specifically sarva-karma-phala-tyāga, 'giving up the fruit of all action', leaving the action itself in place. This distinction governs the whole chapter's argument through verse 12: outright abstention from action (implied by an unqualified saṃnyāsa) is set aside in favor of acting while relinquishing the fruit, the teaching already given at 2.47-51 and repeated through chapters 3-6. Kavayaḥ, 'the wise, the seers', and vicakṣaṇāḥ, 'the discerning', are near-synonyms naming authorities on each side of the definition, not two rival schools.
#3
L: 'To-be-abandoned, as-faulty' — thus some, action, declare, the-wise; 'the-action-of-sacrifice-giving-and-austerity is not to-be-abandoned' — thus others.
I: Some wise men hold that action should be given up as inherently flawed; others say that sacrifice, giving, and austerity should not be given up.
N: A three-verse survey of rival views on renunciation precedes Kṛṣṇa's own verdict at verse 5: eke, 'some', judge all karma doṣavat, 'faulty' (because action inevitably entangles its agent, the very problem the chapter returns to at verses 59-60), and so counsel giving it up outright; apare, 'others', exempt yajña-dāna-tapas, 'sacrifice, giving and austerity', holding these three obligatory regardless. Manīṣiṇaḥ, 'thoughtful men, sages', echoes kavayaḥ/vicakṣaṇāḥ of verse 2.
#4
L: The-verdict hear from-me on-that, on-relinquishment, best-of-the-Bharatas: relinquishment, for, tiger-among-men, threefold [is] proclaimed.
I: Hear my settled conclusion on relinquishment, best of the Bharatas: relinquishment, tiger among men, is said to be of three kinds.
N: Kṛṣṇa sets aside the rival views just surveyed to give his own niścaya, 'settled conclusion, verdict' — a word marking this as the poem's authoritative resolution rather than one more opinion. Bharata-sattama and puruṣa-vyāghra, 'best of the Bharatas' and 'tiger among men', are both epithets of Arjuna. The threefold classification of tyāga announced here is unpacked in verses 7-9 (tāmasa, rājasa, sāttvika tyāga), the first of the guṇa-triads structuring the rest of the chapter.
#5
L: The-action-of-sacrifice-giving-and-austerity not to-be-abandoned; to-be-done indeed, that. Sacrifice, giving, and-indeed austerity, [are] purifying, for-the-wise.
I: The acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity are not to be given up — they are indeed to be performed: sacrifice, giving, and austerity are purifying, even for the wise.
N: Kṛṣṇa states his own position on the disagreement just surveyed: sacrifice, giving and austerity remain kāryam eva, 'indeed to be performed', because they are pāvanāni, 'purifying', even for manīṣiṇām, 'the wise' — who, on the extreme view of verse 3, might be thought to have outgrown the need for them. This settles what, if anything, is to be given up outright, before verse 6 explains how the three should be practiced.
#6
L: These indeed, however, actions, attachment having-abandoned, and-[their]-fruits, are-to-be-done — thus [is] my, Pārtha, settled opinion, the-best.
I: But these very actions should be performed, with attachment and their fruits given up — this, Pārtha, is my settled and highest view.
N: Closes the opening definitional section (verses 2-6): even the obligatory rites just named must be performed with saṅgam ... phalāni ca tyaktvā, 'attachment and their fruits given up' — restating tyāga in verse 2's technical sense (phala-tyāga) as the correct practice, against outright abstention. Niścitam ... matam uttamam, 'my settled and highest opinion', echoes niścayam of verse 4, marking Kṛṣṇa's final word on the question that opened the chapter before he turns, in verses 7-12, to classify tyāga itself by guṇa.
#7
L: Of-prescribed action, however, renunciation not is-fitting; out-of-delusion, its abandonment, tamas-natured, [is] proclaimed.
I: But renunciation of one's prescribed duty is not proper; giving it up out of delusion is declared to be tamas-natured.
N: Opens the tyāga-triad promised at verse 4 (vv. 7-9). Niyatasya karmaṇaḥ saṃnyāsaḥ na upapadyate, 'renunciation of prescribed action is not proper', rejects outright abandonment of one's obligatory duty as such — the same argument chapter 3 already made against total inaction (3.4-8). Mohāt, 'out of delusion', names the motive that makes such abandonment tāmasaḥ, tamas-natured: mistaking the duty itself for a fault, rather than only its fruit.
#8
L: '[It is] painful' — merely thus, whatever action, out-of-fear-of-bodily-affliction, one-should-abandon, he, having-performed rajas-natured relinquishment, not-at-all the-fruit-of-relinquishment would-obtain.
I: If a person gives up some action simply because it is painful, from fear of bodily hardship, he has practiced relinquishment as rajas-natured, and will not gain the fruit of relinquishment at all.
N: The rajas-natured form of tyāga: giving up an action duḥkham iti eva, 'merely because it is painful', out of kāya-kleśa-bhayāt, 'fear of bodily hardship' — avoidance from discomfort rather than understanding — wins none of the tyāga-phalam, 'fruit of relinquishment', named again at verse 12.
#9
L: '[It] is-to-be-done' — merely thus, whatever prescribed action is-performed, Arjuna, attachment having-given-up and-indeed [its] fruit, that relinquishment [is] held sattva-natured.
I: But when a person performs his prescribed action simply because it must be done, Arjuna, giving up attachment and its fruit — that relinquishment is held to be sattva-natured.
N: The sattva-natured form of tyāga: performing niyataṃ karma, 'prescribed action', for no reason but kāryam iti eva, 'because it is simply to be done', while giving up saṅgam ... phalam, 'attachment and the fruit' — the same formula used for sattva-natured sacrifice, austerity and giving throughout chapter 17 (yaṣṭavyam eva iti, dātavyam iti). This is the chapter's positive resolution of the opening debate: not saṃnyāsa (abandoning the action) but this kind of tyāga (abandoning only attachment to its fruit) is truly sattva-natured.
#10
L: Not he-hates unpleasant action, to-the-pleasant not-he-clings — the-renouncer, imbued-with-sattva, intelligent, whose-doubt-is-cut-away,
I: A renouncer who neither hates disagreeable action nor clings to agreeable action, filled with sattva, intelligent, his doubts cut away —
N: A portrait of the sāttvika tyāgī: freedom from dveṣa toward disagreeable duty and from attachment (here read into kuśale na anuṣajjate) toward agreeable duty is what verse 9's ideal looks like in a person, echoing the poem's recurring rāga-dveṣa pairing (3.34, 7.27). Sattva-samāviṣṭaḥ, 'imbued with sattva', and chinna-saṃśayaḥ, 'his doubt cut away' (recalling 4.42's chittvainaṃ saṃśayam), describe the settled clarity such a person has reached; the sentence continues without a break into verse 11.
#11
L: Not, for, by-an-embodied-being possible to-abandon actions entirely; but-who [is] a-relinquisher-of-the-fruit-of-action, he [is] termed 'a-renouncer'.
I: It is not possible for an embodied being to give up action altogether; but whoever gives up the fruit of action is the one truly called a renouncer.
N: A direct restatement, for the agent's own case, of the impossibility of total inaction already argued at 3.5-8: deha-bhṛtā, 'by an embodied being', it simply is not possible to give up action aśeṣataḥ, 'entirely, without remainder'. The only tyāga actually available — and so the only one deserving the name tyāgī — is karma-phala-tyāgī, 'one who relinquishes the fruit of action', the chapter's technical definition from verse 2 now confirmed as the sole workable form of renunciation.
#12
L: Undesired, desired, and mixed — threefold [is] the-fruit of-action; it-comes-about, hereafter, for-non-renouncers; but not at-all for-renouncers.
I: The fruit of action is of three kinds — unwanted, wanted, and mixed — and it comes, after death, to those who have not relinquished it; but never to those who have.
N: Closes the tyāga-section (verses 7-12) by naming what true renunciation wins: ordinary action ripens into aniṣṭam, iṣṭam or miśram phalam, 'bad, good, or mixed fruit', binding a-tyāginām, 'those who do not relinquish [the fruit]', to a future birth (pretya, 'hereafter'), but it does not touch saṃnyāsinām here — meaning those who practice the phala-tyāga just defined, not literal abstainers from action.
#13
L: These-five, great-armed-one, causes, learn from-me: in-Sāṃkhya, in-the-doctrine-of-final-conclusion, [they are] declared, for-the-accomplishment of-all-actions.
I: Learn from me, great-armed one, these five causes taught in Sāṃkhya, the doctrine that traces every act to its conclusion, as necessary for the accomplishment of any action.
N: Opens the chapter's analysis of action's structure (verses 13-19), preparing the ground for the knowledge/action/agent triads of verses 20-28. Sāṃkhye kṛtānte, 'in Sāṃkhya, the doctrine of final conclusions' — kṛtānta, elsewhere 'ordinance, decree', names Sāṃkhya's method of tracing every act back to its complete set of causes. Sāṃkhya is kept untranslated per convention, as at 2.39, 3.3; the five kāraṇāni, 'causes', are enumerated in verse 14.
#14
L: The-seat, likewise the-agent, and the-instrument of-various-kinds, and various distinct-efforts, and-indeed here, fate, the-fifth.
I: The body that is action's seat, the agent, the instrument in its many forms, effort in its many kinds, and, fifth, fate.
N: Names the five kāraṇāni promised in verse 13, the traditional analysis of any completed act: adhiṣṭhāna, 'the seat, the substrate' (the psychophysical body in which action occurs); kartā, 'the agent'; karaṇam pṛthagvidham, 'the instrument, of various kinds' (the sense- and action-organs); vividhāḥ pṛthak ceṣṭāḥ, 'various distinct efforts' (the different exertions accompanying an act); and daivam, 'fate, the divine [factor]' — the element beyond the agent's own control. Verses 15-16 draw the conclusion that no one of these, least of all the self alone, should be mistaken for the sole doer.
#15
L: Whatever action, with-body-speech-and-mind, a-man undertakes, right or wrong, these-five [are] its causes.
I: Whatever action a man undertakes, with body, speech, or mind, whether right or wrong, these five are its causes.
N: Applies the fivefold analysis of verse 14 to any and every act: śarīra-vāṅ-manobhiḥ, 'by body, speech and mind', names the poem's standard threefold instrument of action (cf. the threefold tapas of 17.14-16); nyāyyam vā viparītam vā, 'whether right or wrong', makes clear the analysis holds regardless of the act's moral quality — a structural claim about causation whose ethical payoff follows in verse 16.
#16
L: This being-so, however, who sees the-self alone as-the-agent — because-of-[his]-uncultivated-understanding, he does not [truly] see, the-dull-witted-one.
I: This being so, whoever regards the self alone as the agent, because his understanding is untrained, does not really see; he is dull-witted.
N: Draws the ethical conclusion from the fivefold analysis: given that any action has five contributing causes, one who sees the ātman kevalam, 'the self alone', as kartā, 'the agent', has failed to see correctly, owing to akṛta-buddhitvāt, 'an uncultivated understanding' (buddhi not yet properly trained, echoing kṛtānte of verse 13). Durmatiḥ, 'dull-witted, of perverse judgment', corrects a possible misreading of the poem's own teaching that the self does not act (13.29-31, 5.13-14): that teaching does not mean the self alone should be credited or blamed for worldly action, which always involves the other four causes too.
#17
L: Whose sense-of-'I' is not ego-made, whose understanding is not tainted — even having-killed, he does not kill these people, and is not bound.
I: Whoever's sense of self is free of egoism, whose understanding is untainted — even in killing, he does not kill, and he is not bound.
N: The description of the true knower continues with a positive counterpart to verse 16: one whose bhāvaḥ, 'inner disposition, sense of self', is na ahaṃ-kṛtaḥ, 'not made of ego' (the false identification of self with doer, now shed), and whose buddhi, 'understanding', na lipyate, 'is not tainted' (by the results of action, cf. 5.7, 13.31), even hatvā api, 'even having killed' — recalling the argument of chapter 2 that the true self can neither kill nor be killed (2.19-21) — na hanti, 'does not [truly] kill', na nibadhyate, 'is not bound'. The line answers, from the far side of the teaching, Arjuna's original horror at killing his kinsmen in chapter 1.
#18
L: Knowledge, the-known, the-knower — threefold [is] the-impulse-to-action; the-instrument, the-action, the-agent — thus, threefold [is] the-compendium-of-action.
I: Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower — these three set action in motion; the instrument, the action, and the agent — these three together make up action complete.
N: Opens the chapter's central analytic passage (verses 18-19), pairing two triads: karma-codanā, 'what impels to action' (jñāna, jñeya, parijñātā — knowledge, the known, the knower), and karma-saṃgraha, 'the [full] compendium of action' (karaṇa, karma, kartā — instrument, action, agent). Of these six, jñāna, karma and kartā are each divided threefold by guṇa in what follows (verses 20-28); jñeya and parijñātā are not further subdivided. This verse supplies the vocabulary the rest of the section works through.
#19
L: Knowledge, and action, and-the-agent, threefold indeed, according-to-the-division-of-the-guṇas, [each] is-declared in-the-enumeration-by-guṇa; duly hear those too.
I: Knowledge, action, and the agent are each declared threefold too, according to the division of the guṇas, in this analysis by guṇa — hear these as well, just as they truly are.
N: Announces the three guṇa-triads structuring verses 20-28: jñāna (20-22), karma (23-25), and kartā (26-28), each divided sāttvika/rājasa/tāmasa — the same method chapter 17 applied to faith, worship, food, sacrifice, austerity and giving, now turned on the structure of action just named in verse 18. Guṇa-saṃkhyāne, 'in the enumeration by guṇa', is a common-noun use of saṃkhyāna, 'reckoning, analysis', distinct from (though wordplay on) the proper name Sāṃkhya of verse 13. Yathāvat, 'exactly as it is', promises precision in what follows.
#20
L: By-which one beholds one imperishable essence in-all-beings, undivided among-things-divided — know that knowledge sattva-natured.
I: The knowledge by which a person sees one undying reality in all beings, undivided within things divided — know that to be sattva-natured knowledge.
N: Opens the jñāna-triad (verses 20-22). Ekaṃ bhāvam avyayam, 'one imperishable essence', names the single, changeless reality perceived within sarva-bhūteṣu ... vibhakteṣu, 'all beings ... things divided' — the one self or brahman seen underlying the apparent multiplicity of embodied beings, the poem's recurring vision of unity-in-diversity (cf. 6.29-30, 13.27-28). Avibhaktaṃ vibhakteṣu, 'undivided among the divided', is the verse's central paradox: the object of sāttvika knowledge does not itself fragment even though the bodies it inhabits are many.
#21
L: But the-knowledge which, by-way-of-separateness, manifold-distinct-entities perceives in-all beings — know that knowledge rajas-natured.
I: But knowledge that perceives, through separateness, many distinct beings among all beings — know that to be rajas-natured knowledge.
N: The rajas-natured counterpart to verse 20: pṛthaktvena, 'through separateness', vetti nānā-bhāvān pṛthag-vidhān, 'perceives manifold distinct entities' — knowledge that stops at the plurality of individual beings without discerning the underlying unity, mistaking the many divided forms for many separate realities.
#22
L: But which, as-if-the-whole in-one-single-object, clinging, without-cause, without-grasp-of-the-real-truth, and trifling — that [is] declared tamas-natured.
I: But knowledge that clings to a single thing as if it were everything, without reason, without any grasp of the truth, and petty — that is declared tamas-natured.
N: Closes the jñāna-triad. Kṛtsnavat ekasmin kārye saktam, 'clinging to one single object as if it were the whole', names knowledge trapped at the narrowest possible scope, against verse 20's vision of the one in the many and verse 21's grasp at least of the many themselves. Ahaitukam, 'without cause or reason', and a-tattva-artha-vat alpam, 'without grasp of the true reality, and trifling', complete the triad by naming its lowest form as one that neither reasons nor sees truly nor amounts to much.
#23
L: Prescribed, free-from-attachment, done without-attraction-or-aversion, by-one-not-desiring-the-fruit — the action which [is such], that is called sattva-natured.
I: Action that is prescribed, free from attachment, performed without attraction or aversion, by one who does not desire its fruit — that is called sattva-natured.
N: Opens the karma-triad (verses 23-25), recapitulating the definition of sāttvika tyāga already given at verse 9 and echoing 17.11's aphala-ākāṅkṣibhiḥ: niyatam, 'prescribed' (one's own duty, not chosen from desire); saṅga-rahitam, 'free from attachment'; arāga-dveṣataḥ kṛtam, 'done without attraction or aversion' (the same rāga-dveṣa pairing as verse 10); a-phala-prepsunā, 'by one not desiring the fruit' — together defining action performed exactly as chapters 2-3's core teaching requires.
#24
L: But the action which, by-one-craving-the-fruit-of-desire, or again with-egotism, is-performed with-much-exertion — that [is] declared rajas-natured.
I: But action performed by one driven by desire for its fruit, or again out of egotism, and carried out with great exertion — that is declared rajas-natured.
N: The rajas-natured counterpart: kāma-īpsunā, 'craving [the fruit that satisfies] desire', directly opposes verse 23's a-phala-prepsunā; sa-ahaṃkāreṇa, 'with egotism', names the 'I-am-the-doer' pride already condemned at 3.27; bahula-āyāsam, 'with much exertion', marks such action as effortful and grasping rather than calm.
#25
L: Consequence, loss, harm, without-regard, and [one's-own] capability — the action which, out-of-delusion, is-undertaken, that is called tamas-natured.
I: Action undertaken out of delusion, with no regard for consequence, loss, harm, or one's own capacity — that is called tamas-natured.
N: Closes the karma-triad. Vulgate reads anavekṣya, 'without regard for, without having considered' (an-ava-īkṣ); the BORI critical edition reads anapekṣya, 'without regard for, disregarding' (an-apa-īkṣ), a close synonym from a different preverb — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not adopted here but noted. Anubandham, 'consequence, entanglement', kṣayam, 'loss, ruin', hiṃsām, 'harm [to others]', and pauruṣam, 'one's own strength or capability' are four things the tāmasa agent, acting mohāt, 'out of delusion', simply fails to weigh — the polar opposite of verse 23's carefully considered action.
#26
L: Free-from-attachment, not-given-to-saying-'I', endowed-with-steadfastness-and-zeal, unaffected-in-success-and-failure — [such an] agent is-called sattva-natured.
I: An agent who is free from attachment, does not boast of himself, is full of resolve and zeal, and is unmoved by success or failure — such an agent is called sattva-natured.
N: Opens the kartā-triad (verses 26-28), the third and final triad promised at verse 19. Mukta-saṅgaḥ, 'free from attachment', an-ahaṃ-vādī, 'not asserting "I [am the doer]"', directly answers the ego-driven agent condemned at verses 16-17 and 24; dhṛti-utsāha-samanvitaḥ, 'endowed with steadfastness and zeal' (dhṛti anticipates its own triad at verses 33-35), and nirvikāraḥ siddhi-asiddhyoḥ, 'unmoved in success and failure', recall 2.48's samatvaṃ yoga ucyate. Its visarga is elided with hiatus kept before ucyate, an accepted epic option already seen at 17.14-15.
#27
L: Passionate, desiring-the-fruit-of-action, greedy, of-a-violent-nature, impure, subject-to-elation-and-grief — [such an] agent is-proclaimed rajas-natured.
I: An agent who is passionate, craves the fruit of action, is greedy, violent by nature, impure, and subject to elation and grief — such an agent is proclaimed rajas-natured.
N: The rajas-natured agent: rāgī, 'passionate', karma-phala-prepsuḥ, 'craving the fruit of action', directly opposes verse 26's mukta-saṅgaḥ; lubdhaḥ, 'greedy', hiṃsā-ātmakaḥ, 'violent by nature', aśuciḥ, 'impure', and harṣa-śoka-anvitaḥ, 'given to elation and grief', complete a portrait of an agent wholly at the mercy of circumstance and desire, against verse 26's steadiness in success and failure.
#28
L: Undisciplined, vulgar, obstinate, deceitful, unfaithful, lazy, despondent, and-procrastinating — [such an] agent is-called tamas-natured.
I: An agent who is undisciplined, coarse, arrogant, deceitful, unscrupulous, lazy, prone to despair, and always putting things off — such an agent is called tamas-natured.
N: Closes the kartā-triad and, with it, the whole three-triad analysis of verse 19. Vulgate reads naiṣkṛtikaḥ, 'unfaithful, given to fraud' (from niṣkṛti, 'cheating, breach of agreement'); the BORI critical edition reads naikṛtikaḥ, a close synonym from the related noun nikṛti, 'deceit' — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not adopted here but noted. Ayuktaḥ, 'undisciplined', directly opposes verse 26's steadiness; dīrghasūtrī, literally 'long-threaded', a vivid idiom for chronic procrastination, closes the list. The chapter now turns from the components of action (verses 18-28) to a second guṇa-analysis, of buddhi, dhṛti and sukha (verses 29-39).
#29
L: Of-intellect the-distinction, and-of-steadfastness, according-to-guṇa threefold, hear — being-declared fully, separately, Dhanañjaya.
I: Now hear the threefold division of intellect, and of steadfastness too, according to guṇa, set out fully and point by point, Dhanañjaya.
N: Introduces the second guṇa-analysis of the chapter's central section: buddhi, 'intellect, discernment' (verses 30-32) and dhṛti, 'steadfastness, resolve' (verses 33-35), each divided sāttvika/rājasa/tāmasa as jñāna, karma and kartā already were (verses 20-28); sukha, 'happiness', receives the same treatment immediately after (verses 36-39). Dhanañjaya, 'winner of wealth', a standing epithet of Arjuna.
#30
L: Engagement and cessation, the-to-be-done-and-not-to-be-done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation — which intellect knows, that intellect, Pārtha, [is] sattva-natured.
I: The intellect that knows engagement and withdrawal, what should and should not be done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation — that intellect, Pārtha, is sattva-natured.
N: Opens the buddhi-triad (verses 30-32): pravṛtti and nivṛtti, 'engagement [in action]' and 'withdrawal [from it]' (the two orientations weighed since 3.4-8); kārya and akārya, 'what should and should not be done'; bhaya and abhaya, 'fear and fearlessness' (abhaya itself heads the list of divine qualities at 16.1); and bandha and mokṣa, 'bondage and liberation' — six paired opposites whose correct discrimination is exactly what buddhi is for. Sāttvikī buddhi knows all six pairs truly.
#31
L: By-which [intellect one] discerns dharma and-adharma, and the-to-be-done and-not-to-be-done, not-properly — that intellect, Pārtha, [is] rajas-natured.
I: The intellect that discerns dharma and adharma, and what should and should not be done, but not as they truly are — that intellect, Pārtha, is rajas-natured.
N: The rajas-natured buddhi does not simply fail to discern (that is tamas, verse 32) but discerns ayathāvat, 'not correctly, not as things truly are' — a partial or distorted grasp of dharma and adharma, kārya and akārya, worse than plain ignorance because it passes for genuine understanding.
#32
L: Which, enveloped-by-tamas, judges adharma as-dharma, and all-things as-reversed — that intellect, Pārtha, [is] tamas-natured.
I: The intellect that, shrouded in tamas, takes adharma to be dharma, and takes everything to be the reverse of what it is — that intellect, Pārtha, is tamas-natured.
N: Closes the buddhi-triad: tamasā āvṛtā, 'enveloped by tamas' (the same verb used of ignorance covering knowledge at 5.15, 14.8), inverts dharma and adharma outright rather than merely misjudging them (contrast verse 31's ayathāvat), and takes sarva-arthān viparītān, 'all things as their opposite' — total inversion, the lowest of the three.
#33
L: By-which unwavering resolve, through-yoga, [a person] sustains the-functions-of-mind-breath-and-senses — that steadfastness, Pārtha, [is] sattva-natured.
I: The steadfastness by which a person, through yoga, unwaveringly sustains the functions of mind, breath, and senses — that steadfastness, Pārtha, is sattva-natured.
N: Opens the dhṛti-triad (verses 33-35). Yogena avyabhicāriṇyā, 'through yoga, unwavering' (echoing the unwavering devotion of 13.10's avyabhicāriṇī bhaktiḥ), sustaining manaḥ-prāṇa-indriya-kriyāḥ, 'the functions of mind, breath and the senses' — the full apparatus of the embodied being held steady through disciplined practice, the same picture of yogic self-mastery given at 6.10-14 and echoed later in this chapter's own portrait of the sage (verses 51-53).
#34
L: But by-which resolve [one] holds-to dharma, pleasure, [and] wealth, Arjuna, out-of-attachment, craving-the-fruit — that steadfastness, Pārtha, [is] rajas-natured.
I: But the steadfastness by which a person, out of attachment and craving for reward, holds fast to dharma, pleasure, and wealth, Arjuna — that steadfastness, Pārtha, is rajas-natured.
N: The rajas-natured resolve fastens not on self-mastery but on dharma-kāma-arthān, the traditional trio of worldly aims (with mokṣa, liberation, as the fourth, cf. verse 30's own bandhaṃ mokṣaṃ), pursued prasaṅgena phala-ākāṅkṣī, 'out of attachment, craving the fruit' — resolve harnessed to desire rather than freed from it.
#35
L: By-which, sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and-indeed conceit too, [a] dull-witted [person] does-not let-go — that steadfastness, Pārtha, [is] tamas-natured.
I: The steadfastness, dull-witted as it is, by which a person clings to sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and conceit as well — that steadfastness, Pārtha, is tamas-natured.
N: Closes the dhṛti-triad: tāmasī dhṛti is not steadiness in any positive practice but sheer inability to let go — svapnam, bhayam, śokam, viṣādam, madam, 'sleep, fear, grief, despondency, conceit', the very afflictions verse 30's sāttvikī buddhi was said to discern rightly, now clung to instead of released. Durmedhā, 'dull-witted', closes the description as durmatiḥ closed the description of the false knower at verse 16.
#36
L: But hear from-me now threefold happiness, bull-among-the-Bharatas: wherein [one], through-practice, delights, and reaches the-end-of-suffering,
I: Now hear from me the three kinds of happiness too, bull among the Bharatas: that in which one comes, through practice, to delight, and reaches the end of suffering —
N: Opens the third and final guṇa-triad of the chapter's central section, sukha, 'happiness' (verses 36-39), completing the pair begun with buddhi/dhṛti at verse 29. This verse names only the sāttvika type in outline — abhyāsāt ramate, 'comes to delight through practice' (happiness that must be cultivated, not immediate), and duḥkha-antam ... nigacchati, 'reaches the end of suffering' — with its fuller description following in verse 37; bharata-ṛṣabha, 'bull among the Bharatas', an epithet of Arjuna.
#37
L: That which, at-first, [is] like-poison, [but] in-the-end, like-nectar — that happiness [is] declared sattva-natured, born-of-the-clarity-of-one's-own-understanding.
I: That happiness which is like poison at first but like nectar in the end — that happiness is declared to be sattva-natured, born of the clarity of one's own understanding.
N: Completes the sāttvika type of happiness introduced in verse 36 with the chapter's most memorable image: agre viṣam iva, pariṇāme amṛta-upamam, 'like poison at first, like nectar in the end' — happiness that costs effort or discipline up front but ripens into something like amṛta, 'the nectar of immortality'. Ātma-buddhi-prasāda-jam, 'born of the clarity of one's own understanding', names its true source: not external circumstance but an inwardly settled mind (prasāda recalling the serenity already prized at 2.64-65 and 17.16's manaḥ prasādaḥ).
#38
L: That which, from-the-contact-of-sense-object-and-sense-organ, [is] at-first like-nectar, in-the-end like-poison — that happiness [is] held rajas-natured.
I: The happiness that comes from the contact of the senses with their objects, sweet as nectar at first but like poison in the end — that happiness is held to be rajas-natured.
N: The rajas-natured happiness exactly inverts verse 37's pattern: born of viṣaya-indriya-saṃyogāt, 'the contact of sense-object and sense-organ' (ordinary sensory pleasure, cf. the warning already given at 5.22), it is amṛta-upamam agre, 'like nectar at first', but viṣam iva pariṇāme, 'like poison in the end' — pleasant at the moment of contact but ultimately bitter, the reverse of the sāttvika happiness whose poison-then-nectar order makes it worth the initial cost. The entire first line is one long fused Devanagari token.
#39
L: Which happiness, at-first and-thereafter, [is] deluding to-the-self, arisen-from-sleep-laziness-and-negligence — that is declared tamas-natured.
I: Happiness that deludes the self both at first and in what follows, arising from sleep, laziness, and negligence — that is declared tamas-natured.
N: Closes the sukha-triad, and with it the whole guṇa-analysis begun at verse 29: unlike verses 37-38's happiness that changes character between beginning and end, tāmasa sukha is mohanam ātmanaḥ, 'deluding to the self', agre ca anubandhe ca, 'both at first and thereafter' — deceptive all the way through, its source named outright as nidrā-ālasya-pramāda, 'sleep, laziness and negligence', echoing tāmasī dhṛti's clinging to sleep at verse 35 and the tamas-natured agent's alasaḥ, 'lazy', at verse 28.
#40
L: That does-not exist, on-earth or in-heaven among-the-gods, or again — [any] being free-from-these-three-guṇas-born-of-nature, which by-these would-be.
I: There is no being, on earth or among the gods in heaven, that is free from these three guṇas born of nature.
N: A transitional summary: after three guṇa-triads (jñāna/karma/kartā, buddhi/dhṛti, sukha), Kṛṣṇa states the premise those triads presuppose — that no sattvam, 'being, entity' (the general sense of the word here, distinct from the guṇa sattva just discussed at length, as already flagged at verse 3 and 17.8), pṛthivyāṃ ... divi deveṣu vā, 'on earth or in heaven among the gods', escapes the three prakṛti-jaiḥ guṇaiḥ, 'guṇas born of nature' (prakṛti as the source of the guṇas, per Sāṃkhya doctrine, e.g. 13.19-21, 14.5). This universal claim sets up the following section (verses 41-48), applying guṇa-based classification to the four varṇas' distinct duties.
#41
L: Of-brahmins-kṣatriyas-and-vaiśyas, and-of-śūdras, scorcher-of-the-foe — duties [are] allotted by-the-guṇas arising-from-[their-own]-nature.
I: The duties of brahmins, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas, and of śūdras too, scorcher of the foe, are allotted according to the guṇas born of their own nature.
N: Opens the four-varṇa duty section (verses 41-44), grounding the traditional division of society into brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya and śūdra not in birth as such but in svabhāva-prabhavaiḥ guṇaiḥ, 'the guṇas arising from each person's own nature' — continuing directly from verse 40's claim that all beings are guṇa-bound, and echoing the same grounding of caste in guṇa and karma already given at 4.13 (cātur-varṇyaṃ mayā sṛṣṭaṃ guṇa-karma-vibhāgaśaḥ). Parantapa, 'scorcher of the foe', an epithet of Arjuna.
#42
L: Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, patience, and-indeed uprightness too, knowledge, discernment, [and] faith — [this is] the-brahmin's-duty, born-of-[his-own]-nature.
I: Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, patience, and uprightness, knowledge, insight, and faith — these, born of his own nature, are the brahmin's duty.
N: Names the qualities making up brahma-karma, 'the brahmin's duty' — here brahma stands for brāhmaṇa, 'brahmin', not the untranslated metaphysical brahman used elsewhere in the poem, matching the parallel kṣātraṃ karma, vaiśya-karma and śūdrasya karma of verses 43-44. The nine qualities — śama and dama, 'tranquility of mind and control of the senses' (the pair opening the sthitaprajña's portrait at 2.64ff, named again at 10.4), tapas, śauca, kṣānti, ārjava, jñāna, vijñāna, āstikya, 'faith [in scripture and the unseen]' — are dispositions, not birth-marks, again grounded in svabhāvajam, 'born of one's own nature', picking up verse 41's svabhāva-prabhavaiḥ guṇaiḥ.
#43
L: Heroism, vigor, steadfastness, skill, and-even not-fleeing in-battle, generosity, and-a-commanding-disposition — [this is] the-kṣatriya's duty, born-of-[his-own]-nature.
I: Heroism, vigor, steadfastness, resourcefulness, not fleeing even in battle, generosity, and a commanding presence — these, born of his own nature, are the kṣatriya's duty.
N: Vulgate reads kṣātraṃ karma, adjective plus noun ('kṣatriya-belonging duty'); the BORI critical edition instead compounds the two as kṣatra-karma, 'kṣatriya-duty', reaching the same sense as one word rather than two — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not adopted here but noted. Śaurya, teja, dhṛti, dākṣya, 'heroism, vigor, steadfastness, resourcefulness', yuddhe ca apy apalāyanam, 'not fleeing even in battle', dāna, 'generosity' (the ruler's traditional virtue of largesse), and īśvara-bhāvaḥ, 'a commanding disposition', complete the portrait of the warrior-and-ruler class's native character, again svabhāvajam, 'born of one's own nature'.
#44
L: Farming, cattle-tending, and trade — [this is] the-vaiśya's-duty, born-of-[his-own]-nature; [and] the-duty consisting-in-service [is] the-śūdra's too, born-of-[his-own]-nature.
I: Farming, tending cattle, and trade are the vaiśya's duty, born of his own nature; and service is the śūdra's duty as well, born of his own nature.
N: Closes the four-varṇa section. Vulgate reads kṛṣi-gau-rakṣya-vāṇijyam, using gauḥ (the nominative singular of go, 'cow') itself as a compound member before rakṣya, 'tending'; the BORI critical edition reads the more regular kṛṣi-go-rakṣya-vāṇijyam, with the ordinary compounding stem go- — a real vulgate/BORI variant in the compound's internal form, not a difference of sense ('farming, cattle-rearing and trade' either way), not adopted here but noted. Paricaryā-ātmakam karma, 'duty consisting in service', names the śūdra's role by function (attending on the other three classes) rather than by a list of virtues, unlike the three verses before it; api, 'too, as well', signals that this duty is equally svabhāvajam, 'born of one's own nature' — the section's closing point: all four duties arise from inborn nature rather than external ranking, grounding the argument for the value of one's own duty that follows in verses 45-48.
#45
L: Each-in-his-own duty devoted, accomplishment obtains a-man; devoted-to-his-own-duty, how he-finds accomplishment — that hear.
I: A person devoted to his own duty attains accomplishment; now hear how one devoted to his own duty finds that accomplishment.
N: Opens the chapter's return to the value of one's own duty (verses 45-48), the practical conclusion of the guṇa-based analysis of varṇa-duty just given: sve sve karmaṇi abhirataḥ, 'devoted each to his own duty' (whichever of the four just described applies to him), naraḥ saṃsiddhiṃ labhate, 'a person attains accomplishment' — the poem's recurring argument (already made at 3.35, and again below at 18.47) that spiritual success does not require abandoning one's social role, but performing it rightly. The full answer follows in verse 46.
#46
L: From-whom [is] the-emanation of-beings, by-whom this-all [is] pervaded — him, through-his-own-duty, having-worshipped, a-man attains accomplishment.
I: By worshipping, through his own duty, him from whom all beings arise and by whom this whole universe is pervaded, a person attains accomplishment.
N: Answers verse 45's question by naming the ultimate object of svakarma performed rightly: yataḥ pravṛttir bhūtānām, 'from whom is the emanation of beings' (recalling 7.6, 10.8's ahaṃ sarvasya prabhavaḥ), and yena sarvam idaṃ tatam, 'by whom this whole [universe] is pervaded' (echoing 9.4's mayā tatam idaṃ sarvam) — plainly Kṛṣṇa himself, left here unnamed as tam, 'him'. Sva-karmaṇā tam abhyarcya, 'having worshipped him through his own duty', compresses the whole teaching of karma-yoga (chapters 3-4) into one line: ordinary work, rightly performed, is itself an act of worship.
#47
L: Better, one's-own-dharma, deficient, than-another's-dharma well-performed: doing the-action determined-by-[one's-own]-nature, one-does-not incur sin.
I: One's own dharma, imperfectly done, is better than another's dharma well performed; doing the duty set by one's own nature, a person incurs no sin.
N: Restates the maxim already given at 3.35 (śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ para-dharmāt sv-anuṣṭhitāt — nearly word for word), now placed just after the fourfold varṇa-duty section rather than before Arjuna's own crisis. Sva-dharma, 'one's own dharma' (the duty proper to one's class and inborn nature, as just detailed in verses 41-44), is kept untranslated per convention, in this personal-duty sense distinct from dharma as cosmic order; svabhāva-niyataṃ karma, 'duty fixed by one's own nature', closes the thought with a promise: performing it, whatever its imperfections, incurs no kilbiṣam, 'sin, fault' — the very worry that opened Arjuna's crisis in chapter 1.
#48
L: Inborn duty, Kaunteya, though-flawed, one-should-not abandon; for-all undertakings, by-fault, like-fire by-smoke, [are] enveloped.
I: One should not give up inborn duty, Kaunteya, even though it is flawed; for all undertakings are enveloped by some flaw, as fire is enveloped by smoke.
N: Closes the argument for sva-dharma (verses 45-48) with a memorable simile: sahajaṃ karma, 'inborn duty' (echoing svabhāva-niyataṃ of verse 47), should not be given up sadoṣam api, 'even though flawed', because sarva-ārambhāḥ, 'all undertakings whatsoever' (not only one's own duty, but any action at all), are doṣeṇa āvṛtāḥ, 'enveloped by some flaw', dhūmena agniḥ iva, 'as fire is enveloped by smoke' — imperfection is simply the price of acting in the world, so it cannot be a reason to abandon one's own duty. This closes the chapter's argument (from verse 41) that duty tied to one's own nature, not renunciation of duty, is the right course, and sets up verse 49's turn to the deeper renunciation available even to one who keeps acting.
#49
L: Whose-intellect-is-unattached everywhere, self-conquered, free-from-craving — the-supreme perfection-of-actionlessness, through-renunciation, he-attains.
I: One whose intellect is unattached everywhere, who is self-controlled and free from craving, attains through renunciation the supreme perfection that lies beyond action.
N: Opens the chapter's return to renunciation proper (verses 49-53), now as an inward state compatible with continued action rather than the outright abstention rejected in verses 3-12. Asakta-buddhiḥ sarvatra, 'whose intellect is unattached everywhere' (echoing the ideal already given at 2.57, 5.10), jitātmā, 'self-conquered', vigata-spṛhaḥ, 'free from craving', attains naiṣkarmya-siddhiṃ paramām, 'the supreme perfection of actionlessness' — naiṣkarmya, a state beyond the bondage of action even while perhaps still acting outwardly (cf. 3.4's naiṣkarmyaṃ) — reached saṃnyāsena, 'through [this kind of] renunciation'.
#50
L: One-who-has-attained accomplishment, how brahman he-thus-reaches — learn from-me, in-summary-only, Kaunteya: which [is] the-supreme culmination of-knowledge.
I: Learn from me now, in brief, Kaunteya, how one who has attained that perfection then reaches brahman — the highest culmination of knowledge.
N: Promises to explain the final step: siddhiṃ prāptaḥ, 'one who has attained [that] perfection' just named (naiṣkarmya-siddhi, verse 49), goes on to reach brahma, 'brahman', kept untranslated per convention. Niṣṭhā jñānasya yā parā, 'the supreme culmination of knowledge', recalls the same word niṣṭhā used to ask about types of faith at 17.1, now naming knowledge's own highest resting-point; the description that follows (verses 51-53) is a compressed portrait of the sage's discipline, comparable to 6.10-14's fuller instructions on meditation.
#51
L: Endowed with-intellect, with-purity, and having-restrained the-self with-resolve, and having-abandoned sound-and-other sense-objects, and having-cast-away attraction-and-aversion,
I: Endowed with a pure intellect, restraining himself with resolve, giving up sound and the other sense-objects, and casting away attraction and aversion,
N: Opens the chapter's closing portrait of the sage who reaches brahman (verses 51-53). Vulgate reads buddhyā viśuddhyā yuktaḥ, treating viśuddhi as a noun standing beside buddhyā ('endowed with intellect, with purity'); the BORI critical edition reads buddhyā viśuddhayā yuktaḥ, with viśuddhayā as an adjective agreeing directly with buddhyā ('endowed with a purified intellect') — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not adopted here but noted; the sense differs only slightly either way. Dhṛtyā ātmānaṃ niyamya, 'restraining the self with resolve', śabdādīn viṣayān tyaktvā, 'giving up sound and the other sense-objects' (the objects of the five senses, named by their first member, as at 15.9's śabda-sparśa-rūpa-rasa-gandhāṃś ca), and rāga-dveṣau vyudasya, 'casting away attraction and aversion' (the same pair analyzed throughout the poem, cf. verse 10) begin a chain of gerunds completed only in verse 53's kalpate.
#52
L: Given-to-solitude, eating-little, whose-speech-body-and-mind-are-controlled, intent-on-the-yoga-of-meditation, constantly, dispassion having-taken-refuge-in,
I: Living apart, eating sparingly, controlling speech, body, and mind, always absorbed in the yoga of meditation, taking refuge constantly in dispassion,
N: Continues the ascetic portrait: vivikta-sevī, 'given to solitude' (recalling 6.10's rahasi sthitaḥ ekākī), laghu-āśī, 'eating little' (echoing 6.16-17's yukta-āhāra-vihārasya), yata-vāk-kāya-mānasaḥ, 'controlled in speech, body and mind', dhyāna-yoga-paraḥ, 'given over to the yoga of meditation', nityaṃ vairāgyaṃ samupāśritaḥ, 'constantly resorting to dispassion' (vairāgya paired with abhyāsa as the two pillars of practice at 6.35). The verse remains without a finite verb, continuing the chain of description begun in verse 51 and closed only in verse 53.
#53
L: Egotism, [aggressive] force, arrogance, desire, anger, [and] possessiveness, having-let-go, free-from-'mine', at-peace — for-the-state-of-brahman he-becomes-fit.
I: Having let go of egotism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, and possessiveness, free from the sense of 'mine' and at peace, he becomes fit for identity with brahman.
N: Closes the chain of gerunds begun in verse 51 (niyamya, tyaktvā, vyudasya ... vimucya) with the finite verb kalpate, 'he becomes fit for': having given up ahaṃkāram, balam, darpam, kāmam, krodham, parigraham, 'egotism, [aggressive] force, arrogance, desire, anger and possessiveness' — faults condemned individually elsewhere in the poem (ahaṃkāra at 3.27, kāma-krodha as the twin gate of hell at 16.21) — such a person, nirmamaḥ, 'free from "mine"', śāntaḥ, 'at peace', kalpate brahma-bhūyāya, 'becomes fit for the state of brahman', for identity with brahman. Brahman kept untranslated per convention; this state opens directly, in verse 54, into devotion to Kṛṣṇa himself.
#54
L: One-with-brahman, whose-self-is-serene, he-does-not grieve, he-does-not crave; equal toward-all beings, devotion-to-me he-obtains, supreme.
I: One with brahman, his self serene, he neither grieves nor craves; equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to me.
N: The pivot of the chapter's closing movement: brahma-bhūtaḥ, 'one who has become brahman' (the state just reached in verse 53), prasanna-ātmā, 'serene of self', is described exactly as the sthitaprajña was in chapter 2 (na śocati na kāṅkṣati recalls 2.57) and as equanimous as the ideal yogin of 6.29 (samaḥ sarveṣu bhūteṣu). But rather than stopping at this impersonal attainment, Kṛṣṇa's teaching makes it the doorway to something further: mad-bhaktiṃ ... parām, 'supreme devotion to me' — knowledge of the impersonal absolute culminating not in mere liberation but in bhakti, devotion to the personal Lord, the poem's characteristic synthesis (cf. 7.19's vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti, 14.26-27's brahmaṇo hi pratiṣṭhāham).
#55
L: Through-devotion he-recognizes me, how-great and-who I-am, truly; then, me, truly, having-known, he-enters immediately-thereafter.
I: Through devotion he comes to know me truly, how great I am and who I am; and having known me in truth, he enters into me directly.
N: Explains how the supreme devotion just named (verse 54) itself becomes the means to final knowledge: bhaktyā mām abhijānāti, 'through devotion he comes to know me', yāvān yaḥ ca asmi tattvataḥ, 'how great and who I truly am' (echoing 7.1's yathā māṃ ... jñāsyasi and 10.7's yo vetti tattvataḥ) — devotion, not abstract reasoning, is what finally delivers real knowledge of Kṛṣṇa's nature. Viśate tad-anantaram, 'he enters immediately thereafter', promises the most intimate result the poem offers: not mere approach to Kṛṣṇa but entry into him.
#56
L: All-actions even, always, doing, having-me-as-refuge; through-my-grace, he-obtains the-eternal imperishable state.
I: Even while performing all actions at all times, taking refuge in me, he obtains, through my grace, the eternal, imperishable state.
N: Closes the section begun at verse 49 with the poem's characteristic reconciliation: sarva-karmāṇi api sadā kurvāṇaḥ, 'even performing all actions always', continued action is no obstacle at all once mad-vyapāśrayaḥ, 'taking me as refuge' — the same teaching that opened the chapter's own argument against outright renunciation (verses 5-6, 9). Mat-prasādāt, 'through my grace', names the means by which the śāśvataṃ padam avyayam, 'the eternal, imperishable state' (echoing 8.21's paramaṃ padam and 15.6's paramaṃ mama dhāma), is finally reached — not by the seeker's effort alone — closing the thought before Kṛṣṇa's direct call to surrender begins at verse 57.
#57
L: With-[your]-mind, all-actions, in-me, having-entrusted, devoted-to-me; the-yoga-of-the-intellect having-resorted-to, whose-mind-is-on-me, constantly, be.
I: With your mind, entrust all your actions to me, holding me as the highest; resorting to the yoga of the intellect, keep your thought fixed on me always.
N: Opens the chapter's closing sequence on surrender (verses 57-62), turning from third-person description (verses 49-56) to Kṛṣṇa's direct second-person address. Cetasā sarva-karmāṇi mayi saṃnyasya, 'with your mind entrusting all actions to me' — saṃnyasya, from the same root as saṃnyāsa, the very word defined at the chapter's start (verse 2), now recast as an inward act of dedication rather than outward abstention. Buddhi-yogam upāśritya, 'resorting to the yoga of the intellect' (first named at 2.49), and mat-cittaḥ satatam bhava, 'be one whose mind is on me constantly' (echoing 8.7's mām anusmara yudhya ca), restate the whole poem's teaching in its most direct imperative form.
#58
L: Whose-mind-is-on-me, all-difficulties, through-my-grace, you-will-cross; but if you, out-of-egotism, will-not heed, you-will-perish.
I: With your mind fixed on me, you will cross over every difficulty through my grace; but if out of egotism you do not heed this, you will perish.
N: States both the promise (mat-prasādāt sarva-durgāṇi tariṣyasi, 'through my grace you will cross every difficulty') and the warning (ahaṃkārāt na śroṣyasi vinaṅkṣyasi, 'if out of egotism you do not heed this, you will be lost') framing Kṛṣṇa's call to surrender — the same ahaṃkāra already condemned throughout the chapter (verses 17, 24, 53) now named as the one thing capable of blocking it.
#59
L: As-to-which, relying-on-egotism, 'I-will-not fight' — thus you-think — vain [is] this resolve-of-yours; [your-own] nature will-compel you.
I: If, relying on egotism, you think 'I will not fight' — this resolve of yours is vain; your own nature will compel you.
N: Returns to the poem's opening crisis, quoting almost verbatim Arjuna's own resolve at 2.9's na yotsya iti — there his despair, here named ahaṃkāra, egotism. Mithyā eṣa vyavasāyaḥ te, 'this resolve of yours is false', and prakṛtiḥ tvāṃ niyokṣyati, 'your own nature will compel you', anticipate verse 60's fuller argument that a kṣatriya's inborn nature makes his fighting inevitable regardless of his private wishes.
#60
L: Bound by-[your-own]-duty, born-of-[your-own]-nature, Kaunteya, which, out-of-delusion, you-do-not wish to-do — that, powerless, you-will-do, even against-your-will.
I: Bound by your own duty, born of your own nature, Kaunteya, what you, out of delusion, do not wish to do — that you will do anyway, helplessly, even against your will.
N: Closes the argument begun in verse 59: nibaddhaḥ svena karmaṇā svabhāva-jena, 'bound by your own duty, born of your own nature' (the same svabhāva-niyataṃ karma praised at verse 47, now shown to bind whether one likes it or not), means that yat mohāt kartum na icchasi, 'what, out of delusion, you do not wish to do', tat kariṣyasi avaśaḥ api, 'you will do anyway, even helplessly' — an almost deterministic close to the poem's long argument for freely embracing one's duty: nature will have its way regardless, so wisdom lies in consenting to it rather than resisting.
#61
L: The-Lord, of-all-beings, in-the-region-of-the-heart, Arjuna, dwells, causing-to-revolve all-beings, mounted-on-a-machine, by-[his]-māyā.
I: The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, Arjuna, whirling them about, as if mounted on a machine, by his māyā.
N: The chapter's most vivid image of divine immanence and control: īśvaraḥ sarva-bhūtānāṃ hṛd-deśe tiṣṭhati, 'the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings' (recalling 13.17's sarvasya ca hṛdi sthitam and 15.15's sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi sanniviṣṭaḥ), bhrāmayan sarva-bhūtāni yantra-ārūḍhāni māyayā, 'whirling all beings about, as though mounted on a machine, through māyā' — the machine (yantra), perhaps a water-wheel or puppet-mechanism, a striking image for the compulsion just described in verse 60: beings, seemingly autonomous, are moved by their own nature under the Lord's governance, exactly as māyā was said to operate at 7.14.
#62
L: Him alone, as-refuge, go, with-[your]-whole-being, Bhārata; through-his-grace, supreme peace, [and] the-eternal abode, you-will-attain.
I: Go to him alone as your refuge, Bhārata, with your whole being; through his grace you will attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
N: Closes the surrender sequence (verses 57-62) with a direct command anticipating verse 66's famous mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja: tam eva śaraṇaṃ gaccha sarva-bhāvena, 'go to him alone as refuge, with your whole being' — tam, 'him', referring back to īśvaraḥ of verse 61, i.e. Kṛṣṇa. Tat-prasādāt parāṃ śāntiṃ sthānaṃ ... śāśvatam, 'through his grace, supreme peace and the eternal abode', promises exactly what mat-prasādāt promised at verses 56 and 58 — grace as the means, not the seeker's unaided effort.
#63
L: Thus, to-you, knowledge has-been-declared, more-secret than-[what-is]-secret, by-me; having-considered this fully, as you-wish, so do.
I: Thus I have declared to you knowledge more secret than any secret; reflect on this fully, and then do as you wish.
N: A pivotal verse pausing before the chapter's final, most confidential teaching (verses 64-66): guhyād guhyataram, 'more secret than [what is] secret' (echoing 9.1's guhyatamaṃ and anticipating verse 64's sarva-guhyatamam, 'the most secret of all'), names what has just been taught (the surrender of verses 57-62) as already exceptionally confidential. Vimṛśya etat aśeṣeṇa yathā icchasi tathā kuru, 'having considered this fully, do as you wish', is one of the poem's most striking moments: after everything, Kṛṣṇa explicitly leaves the final choice to Arjuna's own judgment and free will, refusing to compel assent even at the climax of his teaching.
#64
L: The-most-secret-of-all, again, hear my supreme word: 'you-are dear to-me, firmly' — thus; therefore I-will-speak to-you [your] good.
I: Hear again my supreme word, the most secret of all: you are truly dear to me — and so I will tell you what is good for you.
N: Introduces the chapter's very last and most confidential teaching (verses 65-66), building past verse 63's guhyād guhyataram to sarva-guhyatamam, 'the most secret of all'. Iṣṭaḥ asi me dṛḍham iti, 'you are firmly dear to me', gives Kṛṣṇa's own stated motive for the final revelation about to come — not obligation but personal affection for Arjuna — and vakṣyāmi te hitam, 'I will tell you what is good for you', promises the poem's last piece of practical counsel before its climax in verse 66.
#65
L: Whose-mind-is-on-me be, my-devotee, worshipping-me; me do-homage-to; me-alone you-will-come-to — truly, to-you I-promise; dear you-are to-me.
I: Fix your mind on me, be my devotee, worship me, bow down to me; you will come to me alone — this I promise you truly, for you are dear to me.
N: Kṛṣṇa's final personal appeal before the summary verse 66: man-manāḥ, mad-bhaktaḥ, mad-yājī, mām namaskuru, 'fix your mind on me, be my devotee, worship me, bow down to me' — the same fourfold formula already given almost verbatim at 9.34, now repeated at the chapter's climax to bracket the poem's teaching on devotion. Mām eva eṣyasi, 'you will come to me alone', satyaṃ te pratijāne, 'I promise you this is true' — Kṛṣṇa's direct personal guarantee, grounded in priyaḥ asi me, 'you are dear to me', the same bond of affection just named in verse 64.
#66
L: All dharmas having abandoned, to me alone as refuge come; I you from all evils will free — do not grieve.
I: Let go of every duty and come to me as your one refuge. I will free you from all evil; do not grieve.
N: The poem's single most famous verse, traditionally called the carama-śloka, 'final verse [of the teaching]', summing up the whole Gītā in two lines: sarva-dharmān parityajya, 'having abandoned all dharmas' (every dharma whatsoever — not only one's own sva-dharma, so intently argued for earlier in this very chapter, but the whole edifice of duty), mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja, 'come to me alone as refuge' — the culmination of the surrender already urged at verses 57 and 62. Vulgate reads tvāṃ, the ordinary accusative of 'you'; the BORI critical edition reads tvā, an older enclitic accusative form of the same pronoun, identical in sense — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not adopted here but noted. Mā śucaḥ, 'do not grieve', closes the verse by answering Arjuna's very first named affliction (śoka, cf. 2.1's śoka-saṃvigna-mānasam) with Kṛṣṇa's final personal reassurance. This verse's l and i follow the house rendering fixed in conventions.md, drafted fresh from the Sanskrit rather than from any modern published translation, given its extraordinary fame: sarva-dharmān is rendered 'all dharmas' in l (dharma kept visible as the technical term) and 'every duty' in i, per the house text.
#67
L: This, by-you, [is] not-to-be-told to-one-without-austerity, ever, nor to-a-non-devotee, nor to-one-unwilling-to-hear, nor to-whoever is-malicious toward-me.
I: This is not to be told by you to one without discipline, ever, nor to one who is not a devotee, nor to one unwilling to hear it, nor to anyone who is spiteful toward me.
N: Opens the chapter's closing instructions on the confidentiality of the teaching (verses 67-71), naming four kinds of unfit hearer: a-tapaskāya, 'to one without austerity/self-discipline'; a-bhaktāya, 'to a non-devotee'; a-śuśrūṣave, 'to one unwilling to listen respectfully'; and yaḥ mām abhyasūyati, 'whoever is spiteful toward me' (the same malice named of hostile critics elsewhere, cf. 3.32, 9.3's aśraddadhānāḥ). Idaṃ te ... na vācyam, 'this is not to be told by you', uses a dative of agent with the gerundive vācyam, a recognized Sanskrit construction.
#68
L: Who this supreme secret, among-my-devotees, will-declare, having-shown supreme devotion toward-me, to-me-alone he-will-come, without-doubt.
I: Whoever declares this supreme secret among my devotees, having shown supreme devotion toward me, will come to me alone, without doubt.
N: Promises the reward for transmitting the teaching, the positive counterpart to verse 67's restriction: mad-bhakteṣu abhidhāsyati, 'declares it among my devotees' — the correct audience implied negatively there now stated positively. Vulgate reads imam, an alternative masculine-pattern accusative singular of idam agreeing with guhyam by sense rather than strict gender; the BORI critical edition reads the more regular neuter idam, agreeing directly with guhyam — a real vulgate/BORI variant in form only, not a difference of sense, not adopted here but noted. Mām eva eṣyati asaṃśayaḥ, 'he will come to me alone, without doubt', echoes verse 65's identical promise (mām eva eṣyasi satyaṃ), now extended to the teacher of the teaching as well as to its original recipient.
#69
L: And, than-him, among-human-beings, no-one to-me [is] doing-what-is-most-dear; nor, to-me, than-him, another dearer will-be, on-earth.
I: And there is no one among human beings who does me more dear service than he; nor will anyone else on earth be dearer to me than he.
N: Ranks the teacher of verse 68 above all others in Kṛṣṇa's regard: kaścit me priya-kṛttamaḥ, 'anyone more dear-service-doing to me' (priya-kṛttama, a superlative naming the highest degree of pleasing service), na bhavitā, 'nor will there be', tasmāt anyaḥ priyataraḥ bhuvi, 'anyone else dearer on earth'. The double negative (na ... na ca) presses the claim from both present and future.
#70
L: And who will-study this righteous dialogue of-us-two, by-that, by-the-sacrifice-of-knowledge, I would-be worshipped — thus [is] my opinion.
I: And whoever studies this righteous dialogue between the two of us will, by that sacrifice of knowledge, have worshipped me, or so I hold.
N: Extends the promise beyond the original teacher/disciple pair to future students of the text itself: adhyeṣyate ... yaḥ imaṃ dharmyaṃ saṃvādam āvayoḥ, 'whoever will study this righteous dialogue of ours' — the Gītā's own dialogue, referred to here within itself. Jñāna-yajñena, 'by the sacrifice of knowledge' (echoing 4.33's ranking of jñāna-yajña above material sacrifice), tena aham iṣṭaḥ syām iti me matiḥ, 'by that I would be worshipped, in my view' — mere study of the teaching, undertaken in that spirit, itself counts as worship.
#71
L: And a-man having-faith, free-from-malice, who would-even hear [it] — he too, freed, the-auspicious worlds of-those-of-virtuous-deeds would-attain.
I: And even a man who merely hears it, with faith and without malice, is freed as well, and attains the fair worlds of those of virtuous deeds.
N: Closes the confidentiality section (verses 67-71) by extending the promise to the simplest possible engagement with the teaching: śraddhāvān an-asūyaḥ ... yaḥ naraḥ śṛṇuyāt api, 'even a man who merely hears it, with faith and without malice' (an-asūyaḥ directly answering verse 67's warning against yaḥ mām abhyasūyati, 'whoever is spiteful toward me'), saḥ api muktaḥ, 'he too is freed', reaching śubhān lokān puṇya-karmaṇām, 'the fair worlds of those of virtuous deeds' — a lesser but still substantial reward for the listener alone, below the teacher's promise of coming to Kṛṣṇa himself at verse 68. This closes the run of promises begun at verse 68, before Kṛṣṇa turns, in verse 72, to ask Arjuna directly whether the teaching has taken hold.
#72
L: Has-this been-heard, Pārtha, by-you, with-one-pointed mind? Has-the-delusion-of-ignorance been-destroyed, of-yours, Dhanañjaya?
I: Has this been heard by you, Pārtha, with a one-pointed mind? Has the delusion born of ignorance been destroyed for you, Dhanañjaya?
N: Kṛṣṇa's own question, closing the teaching before Arjuna's final reply (verse 73): kaccit etat śrutam tvayā eka-agreṇa cetasā, 'has this been heard by you with a one-pointed mind?' — echoing the concentration urged throughout (e.g. 6.12's ekāgraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā) — and kaccit ajñāna-saṃmohaḥ pranaṣṭaḥ te, 'has the delusion of ignorance been destroyed for you?', asking directly whether the very saṃmoha that opened the poem (cf. 1.30) has been dispelled by everything taught since. This personal check-in, rare in the poem's structure, marks the teaching as essentially complete.
#73
L: Destroyed, [my] delusion; memory regained, by-me, through-your-grace, Acyuta; established I-am, my-doubt-gone; I-will-do [your] word, yours.
I: My delusion is destroyed; I have regained memory through your grace, Acyuta. I stand firm, my doubts gone; I will act on your word.
N: Arjuna's final response closes his own arc of the poem: naṣṭo mohaḥ, 'delusion is destroyed', directly answers Kṛṣṇa's question at verse 72. Smṛtir labdhā, 'memory has been regained' (recalling smṛti-bhraṃśa, 'the loss of memory', the last stage of desire's ruin named at 2.63), names the recovery of Arjuna's own clear understanding of his duty, obscured since chapter 1's grief. Sthitaḥ asmi gata-sandehaḥ, 'I am established, my doubt gone', and kariṣye vacanaṃ tava, 'I will act on your word', give Arjuna's own resolution — not mere intellectual agreement but a stated commitment to act, closing the frame-question of renunciation-versus-action with which the chapter itself began. Acyuta, 'the unfallen', an epithet of Kṛṣṇa (cf. 1.21).
#74
L: Thus, I, of-Vāsudeva and-of-Pārtha, the-great-souled, this-dialogue, I-heard, wondrous, hair-raising.
I: Thus have I heard this wondrous, hair-raising dialogue between Vāsudeva and the great-souled Pārtha.
N: Sañjaya's own voice returns after the dialogue proper ends, opening the chapter's closing frame (verses 74-78), which mirrors the poem's opening frame in chapter 1. Vāsudevasya pārthasya ca mahā-ātmanaḥ, 'of Vāsudeva and of the great-souled Pārtha', names both speakers by patronymic: Vāsudeva, 'son of Vasudeva', an epithet of Kṛṣṇa; Pārtha, 'son of Pṛthā', Arjuna. Adbhutam, 'wondrous', roma-harṣaṇam, 'hair-raising' (the same physical response to awe already described at 1.29 and throughout chapter 11's theophany, e.g. 11.14), names Sañjaya's own reaction as witness.
#75
L: Through-the-grace-of-Vyāsa, this supreme secret I-have-heard, [and this] yoga, from-Kṛṣṇa-the-Lord-of-yoga speaking directly, himself.
I: Through Vyāsa's grace I have heard this supreme secret, this yoga, directly from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga, speaking himself, in person.
N: Sañjaya names the source of his own extraordinary knowledge: vyāsa-prasādāt, 'through the grace of Vyāsa' (the sage traditionally credited with composing the whole Mahābhārata, said to have granted Sañjaya the divine sight to witness the distant battlefield), enabling him to hear etat guhyam param, 'this supreme secret', yogam, 'yoga' — the poem's whole teaching named simply as yoga at its very close — sākṣāt, 'directly, in person', from yoga-īśvarāt kṛṣṇāt, 'from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga' (echoing 11.4's yogeśvara), kathayataḥ svayam, 'speaking it himself'. This closes the chain of transmission the chapter has traced since verse 70's teacher-to-student promise.
#76
L: O-king, having-remembered again-and-again this-wondrous dialogue, of-Keśava-and-Arjuna, sacred, I-thrill, again-and-again.
I: O king, remembering again and again this wondrous, sacred dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I thrill with joy again and again.
N: Opens Sañjaya's closing personal testimony (verses 76-78), addressed directly to Dhṛtarāṣṭra (rājan, resuming the frame that opened the whole poem at 1.1). Saṃsmṛtya saṃsmṛtya, 'remembering again and again' (a doubled gerund for repeated action, in the manner of yadā yadā at 4.7), and hṛṣyāmi ... muhur muhuḥ, 'I thrill again and again', name Sañjaya's own continuing rapture at having witnessed the dialogue; puṇyam, 'sacred, holy', echoes adbhutam of verse 74. Keśava and Arjuna name the two interlocutors again, now by their more intimate epic names rather than verse 74's formal patronymics.
#77
L: And-that, having-remembered again-and-again, the-form, exceedingly-wondrous, of-Hari — great [is] my astonishment, king; I-thrill again and-again.
I: And remembering again and again that exceedingly wondrous form of Hari, my astonishment is great, O king; I thrill with joy again and again.
N: Continues Sañjaya's testimony, now recalling specifically rūpam ati-adbhutam hareḥ, 'the exceedingly wondrous form of Hari' — the universal form (viśva-rūpa) revealed in chapter 11, singled out here as the single most astonishing thing witnessed. Vismayaḥ ... mahān, 'great astonishment', and hṛṣyāmi ca punaḥ punaḥ, 'I thrill again and again' (echoing verse 76's muhur muhuḥ), close the personal reflection before the poem's final verse turns from Sañjaya's own feeling to a formal blessing. Hari, a name of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, used here for the first time in this chapter.
#78
L: Where the-Lord-of-yoga, Kṛṣṇa, [is], where Pārtha, the-bow-bearer, [is] — there, splendor, victory, prosperity, [and] firm right-conduct — [this is] my conviction.
I: Where Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga, is, and where Pārtha, the archer, is — there, I am convinced, are splendor, victory, prosperity, and firm right conduct.
N: The Gītā's closing verse, Sañjaya's own final judgment rather than any word of Kṛṣṇa or Arjuna: yatra yoga-īśvaraḥ kṛṣṇaḥ, yatra pārthaḥ dhanur-dharaḥ, 'where Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga, is, where Pārtha, the bow-bearer, is' — naming Kṛṣṇa by the same epithet just used at verse 75 and Arjuna by his warrior's role. Tatra śrīḥ vijayaḥ bhūtiḥ dhruvā nītiḥ, 'there splendor, victory, prosperity, and firm right conduct', names four goods together — dhruvā, 'firm, sure', may modify nīti alone or, more likely, the whole preceding list. Matir mama, 'this is my conviction', closes the entire eighteen-chapter poem not with a divine pronouncement but with the narrator's own considered judgment — Sañjaya, the once-neutral reporter of chapter 1, ending as a believer.
